doc.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 23, 2003 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Contractors, midnight calls and Radio Registry
summary: How session work was booked by contractors phoning at night and through the Radio Registry answering service.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: That’s cool. How did you handle the business end of it? You know in these days of agents and cell phones and pagers and all that kind of stuff it’s a little different. How did you get the word to report to a certain place, and how did you set your dates.
Well they would call my house, say at midnight, and say we’re doing a date tomorrow at two, two to five. I’d say I’ll be there. A contractor would call me.
He’d call your house at midnight?
Yeah. Yeah. And sometimes a contractor would call on Sunday night and give you like four dates for the week, all at Columbia Records see. This one, this one and that one. Okay, I’ll be there.
And if you weren’t available then he’d go down to the next person?
Well he’d get somebody else. Yeah.
Was there some kind of — I forget the name of it — some kind of service that, maybe that’s what you’re talking about.
Oh well that was a telephone service. Radio Registry.

If you had Radio Registry, there was so much work around that the contractor would just call Radio Registry and tell him who to call see? And then they would call you. So I was with Radio Registry too you know. But then it got a little mixed up because sometimes they’d call other guys instead of calling you. They’d tell the contractor well he was busy and I wasn’t you know.
Hmm. Wonder why they were doing that? And did you actually live in New York?
